metadata.title: The predictive validity of PIRLS and ePIRLS on later academic achievement: Insights from Sweden,

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PIRLS and ePIRLS reading scores from grade 4 and relates them to later teacher-assigned grades and GPAs in grades 6 and 9 in Sweden. The provided text does not report any complex survey design details (e.g., stratification/cluster variables) or whether PIRLS/ePIRLS sampling weights were applied in the regression models. The analyses are described as being performed in SPSS and Mplus, but no weight variable names (e.g., TOTWGT/W_FSTUWT) or replicate-weight procedures are mentioned, so the weighting approach cannot be confirmed from the excerpt. For replication with the original PIRLS/ePIRLS microdata, analysts should use the official PIRLS/ePIRLS student sampling weights and, if available, replicate weights recommended by the PIRLS technical documentation to obtain design-correct standard errors.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The paper states that PIRLS and ePIRLS are IRT-scaled latent models based on plausible values, but it does not describe how plausible values were combined in the regression analyses (e.g., Rubin’s rules vs. averaging). It also does not report any explicit missing-data strategy for the analytic variables (reading scores, grades, and demographic controls). Given that the study relies on multiple latent/score components and regression models, the absence of PV and missing-data documentation is a reporting gap that limits reproducibility and may affect standard errors and effect estimates.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The study focuses on Sweden and examines students’ grade-4 reading performance using both paper-based PIRLS and the computer-based ePIRLS (digital mode), then predicts later academic outcomes using teacher-assigned grades in Swedish, Mathematics, and English plus GPA in grades 6 and 9. The excerpt does not specify additional inclusion/exclusion rules (e.g., whether only students with both modes administered were retained, whether ePIRLS participation was restricted to the subset of schools/students who took the digital assessment, or any missing-data exclusions). Therefore, the analytic sample is not fully identifiable from the provided text; at minimum, it includes students with available PIRLS/ePIRLS scores and later grade/GPA outcomes in the specified grades.

main_findings.dataset_used: PIRLS 2016 Grade 4 Reading (paper) and ePIRLS 2016 Grade 4 Reading (digital), Sweden
main_findings.performance_metrics: Correlations: PIRLS–Swe6 r=.600; ePIRLS–Swe6 r=.619. Regression (standardized Beta, SE): Model 1 Mean β=.630(.013)*; Model 2 Difference β=.050(.020)*; Model 3 Gender β=.214(.014)*; Parental education β=.079(.017)*; Home language β=-.017(.017) (ns). R²: Model 1 .397; Model 2 .399; Model 3 .450.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PIRLS 2016 Grade 4 Reading (paper) and ePIRLS 2016 Grade 4 Reading (digital) data in Sweden, the study leveraged mean reading achievement and the digital–paper difference score (plus demographic controls) to predict Swedish grades in Grade 6, finding that mean reading achievement was a strong predictor (β≈.630) and that the digital advantage added a small but significant incremental effect (Difference β≈.050). This indicates that digital reading performance captures additional competencies that translate into slightly higher short-term language achievement, supporting the use of digital assessments for predictive monitoring while still accounting for mode effects.

data.outcome_summary: This study uses PIRLS 2016 Grade 4 reading scores (paper-based PIRLS and computer-based ePIRLS) in Sweden and examines how they predict later academic achievement measured as teacher-assigned grades in Swedish, English, and Mathematics plus GPA in grades 6 and 9. The results show moderate-to-strong correlations between early reading and later outcomes, with ePIRLS correlations generally slightly higher than PIRLS. In regression models, mean reading achievement is a consistent predictor across subjects and grades (e.g., Swedish Grade 6 β=.630; English Grade 9 β=.568; Mathematics Grade 9 β=.504; GPA Grade 9 β=.510). Adding the digital–paper difference (ePIRLS minus PIRLS) yields small incremental predictive effects mainly for language subjects in grade 6 and for Swedish/English in grade 9, while the digital advantage is not significant for Mathematics and GPA in grade 9. Limitations include optional ePIRLS participation (self-selection) and the lack of reported PV-combination and missing-data handling details, which constrains reproducibility and interpretation of effect sizes.
